utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Madam Registrar, call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-99-36-T, the Prosecutor versus Radoslav Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Brdjanin, can you hear me in a language that you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning. I can hear and understand. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. You may sit down. Appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, Joanna Korner, Ann Sutherland, assisted by Denise Gustin, case manager. Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you. Appearances for Radoslav Brdjanin?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours, I'm John Ackerman with Milan Trbojevic and Marela Jevtovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And good morning to you, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Colonel, good morning to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are proceeding with your testimony this morning. Before we do so, please could you repeat your solemn declaration? Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. You may sit down and Ms. Korner will be proceeding with her questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. I wonder if Colonel Selak could have back the document he was looking at yesterday which is P1574.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Colonel Selak, could you turn, please, to the page we were looking at yesterday evening, which is I'm sorry, I should tell you it's the part headed "some experiences" which is our page 5.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The paragraph -- we dealt with the fact that, as you explained to us, that the political leadership, the municipal leaders, did have an effect on the army when it -- certainly in respect of the troop replenishment, and the next paragraph reads, "Some activists, some working bodies of the region and various assemblies in the Serbian Autonomous Regions are presenting the army with conditions or ultimatums advocating the subordination of army units to their commands in smaller areas." Et cetera. And we'll see in a later document some examples of that. Due to such occurrences certain specific measures have been taken but these problems will soon be discussed with SDS leaders in Sarajevo, because if any of these volunteer units get out of hand, this may lead to serious consequences." Now, Colonel, I'm going to look at a document in a moment that deals with what exactly these volunteer units were. But working on the basis that they are some kind of paramilitary organisations, were you aware from what happened of such units getting out of hand?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Such units or groups of persons, paramilitary organisations, once they get their hands on weapons and military equipment, and if there is no control, then they do whatever they had set out to do. And that is, the arrest and mistreatment of persons, ethnical cleansing, killing, plunder, from other ethnic groups. That is to say Bosniak, Croats, and others too.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: As an experienced army officer, would you expect that this was something that was foreseeable, that if you armed people like this, they would start getting out of control, as it's put, and as you've described?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The army consciously gave weapons to these people and that was shown from the previous surveys. The army could have had control over these groups and it was duty-bound to have control over them. Just as the sociopolitical community, the municipality, was duty-bound to do that. The Ministry of the Interior, the police organs, the authorities in the municipality as well. Nevertheless, there was a joint objective involved, so the army did not intervene and it is precisely in order to have this joint objective carried out, and that is the ethnic cleansing of the area involved. They explained that this was under quotation marks "the protection of Serbs from genocide." However, other peoples did not have such protection and weapons were not given to them. That was the policy of the SDS and the policy of the authorities of Republika Srpska at that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I appreciate your saying from your knowledge that this was obviously an agreement, part of the plan, but would it be foreseeable to anybody in -- as a military officer, that you armed people like this, they were likely to go and commit the crimes that you've described?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: As a professional officer, and at that time I was living in the area too, where all of this was going on, I was horrified by what was actually done. That is to say that arms were issued to people in an unauthorized manner without any control. Now, what would these people do? We have to be aware of the fact that there were people under the influence of alcohol there, people who were nervous, people who were in that kind of psychological condition when they committed crimes. That had to be foreseen. There were laws in Yugoslavia, military laws, which made it compulsory for officers to behave in a lawful manner in peace time and even more so in times of war. I personally, as commander of a unit, would have arrested my officer who would have allowed such things to happen and who would have issued weapons to persons in this way without any control. I would have taken adequate disciplinary measures.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Colonel. Can we move, then, finally, on this document, please, to the paragraph, it's on our page 6, that begins, "For the time being, it is necessary to halt the formation and arming of volunteer units until the situation in the already-established units is sorted out and until some information and solutions are found. After that, a decision must be made on whether to continue with the establishment of units or not." Now, this was written, a report written, in March, 1992. You've described how you were aware that these -- the Serbs were being armed. To your knowledge, did the arming stop between then and April?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The arming of these paramilitary units or as they say volunteer units continued. It was done all the time while I stayed in Banja Luka, and that is to say the 18th of May, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And finally, on this document, because I don't want to come back to unless it's necessary, page 8, please. They described -- it's page 8, sorry, in the English translation. It's part of paragraph 7, "Garrisons in some part of Bosnia-Herzegovina and prospects for their remaining there." And there is a paragraph that reads, "In the light of the option whereby Bosnia and Herzegovina will soon be recognised as a state, and the fact that the Serbian people do not want to remain there and live in a ghetto state, it is to be expected that the JNA will face many problems." Do you know what problems the author of this document had in mind? Obviously, you can't know what he had in mind, General Kukanjac, but what was the problems that were foreseen whilst you were still a member of the JNA as a result of what was happening?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It says that it was suspected already at that time that officers who were Croats and officers who were Muslims, Bosniaks, could not stay in the army because this army had to be Serb under the control of the Serb people, and it is precisely this attitude towards these officers, or rather the Serb leadership was afraid that these officers would not want to carry out the tasks that would be put before them, and an effort was made, and it ultimately proved to be successful to remove them from the army.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: So it was required that the army be under the control of the Serb people, or rather the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Colonel Selak. You can give that document back and can you now look, please, at a document that was attachment 5.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But , Your Honour, in fact, we had a number of versions of this document and it was pointed out to me this morning it's already been exhibited as P15, and I think we better have a look at that, because, Your Honour, there is an extra letter attached to this document. It was attachment 5 to the Colonel's second -- statement of the 10th of March, but there is a fuller version with a letter attached at P15. Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, in fact, this goes back to August, 1991, but it is a detailed account of these so-called volunteer units. The letter that I want the colonel to look at first of all is this one.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, we are having some difficulty finding it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm going to ask for the English version to be put on to the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Does it have a disclosure number or anything like that that we could use?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, 1.120. But it's only the letter that's not -- the second part of the document is -- was attached, is attachment 5.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If I am reading you well, Ms. Korner, is that we do have an attachment 5 together with the second statement without however the letter, the covering letter.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Exactly, that's it, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So that the letter should be in document or in Exhibit P15 if I read you well?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It is, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do we need it or --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, I'm just going to ask.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: To put it on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's on the ELMO now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Because you did mention August, 1991, while the attachment that we have is dated the 27th May, then.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. If Your Honour looks at attachment 5, which bears the numbers 01902 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, that's a different one.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Attachment 5 to the statement of the 10th of March, and it's actually been -- you'll see at the top-handwritten a signature on the 10th of March, 2001 that's purely, I think --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So it's not the second statement. We'll find it, don't worry.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We'll find it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Colonel Selak, this is a letter addressed to the command of the Bosanska Krajina volunteer units, Banja Luka, 24th of August, 1991, to the municipal staffs of volunteer units, and it's signed, the letter, "Commander, Colonel Ostoja, Djukanovic [phoen], I think it is?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dejanovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Dejanovic. Do you know who that was?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This officer came from somewhere else. He was not a serving officer in Banja Luka, and this is the first time I hear of this gentleman, Mr. Dejanovic. I see that he writes in Cyrillic. I believe that he came to Bosnia from elsewhere, from Serbia, say. Well, anyway, this is the first time I hear of him, so I have no comment.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: In that case, you mean you're guessing because he wrote in Cyrillic he comes from Serbia. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not necessarily. However, most officers who came from those parts signed their name in Cyrillic. Allow me to mention the following as well: In 1995 in my command, there were Serbs, my subordinate officers who were in their offices and there were sheets of paper on their desk and they were practising their Cyrillic. They were practising their signatures in Cyrillic which obviously shows that the Latin alphabet was the official alphabet but this was an individual thing, a sort of personal thing. It varied from one person to another.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Just pause for a moment, Colonel. The translation came, as you are saying, in 1995 in your command. Did you say that?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: 1991, 1991, in my command, there were officers who were practising to sign their names in the Cyrillic alphabet.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Can we just briefly look at what this gentleman is saying? He encloses what he describes or what's translated as an essay. Could you just read, please, the first part of that sentence after, "To the municipal staffs," just the very first part, just read. If you can read it.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: "We hereby enclose the report submitted at the session of the representatives of the municipalities of Bosanska Krajina on the occasion of the establishment of the command of volunteer units of Bosanska Krajina."

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. All right. We see that it describes what's going to be set out in the document that we are going to look at. And says that all the documents you receive from this command are to be labelled as strictly confidential and treated as such. And so on. And so forth. Now, before we look at the document that's enclosed, had you ever heard of this organisation, the command of Bosanska Krajina volunteer units, in August of 1991?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In August of 1991, I had not heard of this command or did I know where their headquarters were. I lived in Banja Luka. I worked in Banja Luka. But I had no knowledge of this command.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: After all, it says here, "Strictly confidential." So it was secret.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Can we now look at the document, please, that was enclosed? On the version --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I just explain so that Your Honour understands, the signature and the top and the date, the 10th of March, is in fact the colonel's, if you're looking at attachment 5 now because he was asked to sign just to show that he was given the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The objectives and principles of organising volunteer units in the Bosanska Krajina area. Then it sets out the reason for this unit and says, "The JNA does not have sufficient forces to cover and protect all inhabited places. In the event, in view of historical memory and real danger, this people must organise their own volunteer units for their own defence and protect lives. This must be done, however, on the principles of Territorial Defence. In conformity with the law on all people's defence, that is to say they be a constituent part of the armed forces of the socialist or federal Republic of Yugoslavia as a form of the armed Serbian people and can be nothing else. The Serbian people have no other army except the JNA and they consider it their own. Just as they consider it their duty to defend their common state from all those intent on destroying it or who are opposed to equality and coexistence in the same state." Were you aware of the -- at any stage, after this date, and before you left the JNA, of a volunteer unit that was a constituent part of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not aware of a single volunteer unit that was within the formation of JNA units.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew of their existence, though, and I knew what their role was Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. in that area. And I knew that the army had to have influence over them because it armed them, it trained them, and these units carried out the tasks that the army did not have time to carry out or could not carry out.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Well, let's very quickly, because I think the document explains itself, the difference between these and the TO is they would be established on an ethnic basis comprise only one nation, until an agreement is reached between the peoples who wished to live in a common state, free and equal." And then I don't think we need bother with the rest. "It is suggested that the volunteer units have the exclusive task of protecting the people from massacre by enemy forces which irrationally hate the Serbian people. Our volunteer units will never be deployed against another people. They will have an exclusively defensive role." I think this can be answered very simply, Colonel Selak, yes or no, from what you know of these forces, is that, in fact, what happened, that they played nothing more than a defensive role?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you. "The volunteer units will accept all tasks issued by the JNA units which they can execute in conformity with the extent which they are armed and their level of organisation and which pertain to the protection of a common state, peace and the freedom and equality of peoples which wish to live in a joint democratic state. Could never and shall never execute tasks to the detriment of the Serbian people," et cetera. Then, "Proposals for organising the command, the emphasis is on the command, since this is a broader concept than a staff, while a staff is a constituent part of every command?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I have no idea what document we are referring to. The usher can't find it. It's not on the ELMO. I don't know if Your Honours have it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Of course we do, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Is it in the packet that the Prosecutor gave you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. The ERN number is 01902021. That's the first page of this attachment. And Ms. Korner was -- has been reading from page 1 and then she moved --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: About to move, Your Honour, to the next page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I don't know. If the usher is having problems.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Perhaps, Mr. Ackerman, if you have an extra copy, or else I could give my own copy to the Defence and then they will return it later.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can I continue? I think the usher has it now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I still don't have it, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, it's now on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, I should add so that normally we only give the Defence the list, but this time we thought in order to prevent this from happening we will give them copies as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, what they gave us is right here and we didn't take it anywhere, it stayed in the building all night, we are going through it, we can't find it. And I'm sorry, I can't find it. I wish I could find it, Your Honour, and solve all this problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman, there are various statements. You have to go to the statement of the 10th of March, 2001. And then there you have one to eight as attachments and we are talking of attachment number 5.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: In any event, Your Honour, it's on the ELMO it's also the same as P15 so... Right. Could we go, then, please, usher to the next page, page 2 on the ELMO?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Where they set out their command structure. It should have commander a deputy commander, a member of the command, a prominent figure of the SDS party, a highly political figure. Then a Chief of Staff and so on and so forth. And a, chief of the police. That is to say of the SUP for Bosanska Krajina. "As opposed to other similar commands of JNA units, the specific character of the member of the command, a prominent figure of the SDS is noteworthy. This individual is de facto the principal coordinator of official SDS policy as the most organised political force of the Serbian people which expresses the interests of its people in the most complete manner possible. Without the SDS as the main political organiser of the Serbian people, this command could not fulfil its role. That is to say, achieve close ties with the people, which is of the greatest significance in today's political situation. The chief of the Bosanska Krajina SUP is indispensable in the command from a different, security aspect, because the security situation in the territory can only be ensured by uniting forces." Now, within the JNA, colonel, were politicians or police officers actual members of units?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: In what sense?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the unit formation, in the command was the deputy for morale and political affairs, in each unit, and he answered only to the commander. His task was to work to raise the morale in the subordinated units, the morale of the soldiers and the whole unit, and these organs were regularly in touch with the political organs of the sociopolitical community in whose area they were.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. I'm sorry, it's my fault. I didn't put the question properly. We know that, because we looked at your list of functions within the JNA, there was an officer for morale and there was a security officer. But were these police officers -- was that -- was the sorry, -- was the deputy for morale a politician or was he a serving JNA officer? Was the person for security a police officer or a serving JNA officer?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those were active officers who were carrying out security and political duties within the units. They had special training, from their specialty. They completed the regular military academies and later, in accordance with their duties, they went to different courses, seminars, workshops, and so on, and dealt only with those issues. That was their specialty.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But here, what appears to be suggested, anyhow, is that an actual politician and an actual police officer should be incorporated into the units. Did that ever happen within the JNA, that actual politicians, SDS, in JNA units? Not volunteer, but JNA units?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I want to come back to the end of my questioning to the relationship between the army, and the political, as you've expressed it. All right. Then it goes on to deal with various other requirements of the forces which I don't intend to go through. If we go to page 3 in the translation --

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I just give an additional explanation about what I said earlier? When I said that active officers carried out those duties, however, in war, after mobilisation, it was possible to have some reserve officer perform that duty, but as an officer, they could be of other specialties, even politicians, but it could happen in certain circumstances that they would be politicians as well as carry out those duties, and I apologise because I forgot to say that earlier.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That's quite all right. And I think we all understand the distinction. All right. If we look, please, could you go to the paragraph in your version of the document that begins, "Persons loyal to their people are needed here"? It's on our page 3 in the middle of the second paragraph. "Persons loyal to their people are needed here."

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: "That is to say those who will not accept terms under which" --

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. Just one moment. Yes, yes, that's okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: "Persons loyal to their people are needed here. That is to say those who will not accept terms under which the Serbs must lose out so that other peoples may only then wish to live with them in a common state. Under no circumstances will anyone be able to proclaim that we are paramilitary forces or declare us Serbian nationalists. Not even hypothetically will they be able to turn us into Chetniks, terrorists, and the destroyers of the state for which it was precisely the Serbian people who gave the most lives." The paramilitary groups that we know operated during the conflict, did you hear them described at any stage as Chetniks or terrorists?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I heard several times that they were called Chetniks, terrorists, slaughterers and other derogatory terms. This is probably a result of their behaviour, based on that, the term "Chetnik" became synonymous with those units. Unfortunately, there was a lot of behaviour like that, and the result is well known.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And then it explains that the principle would be one, as the Swiss system, you work and defend yourself, and finishes off by saying that: "Weapons are the safest in the hands of our Serbian men. They clean it, safeguard it, and maintain it with a sense of responsibility. They have a psychological relationship with it which is very different from weapons newly obtained from a mobilisation assembly points." And then it points out that, "A poor level of training can be swiftly compensated for if organised activity is pursued and assist tell of defending the people is inexpensive." And then finally this, on the last paragraph of this document, page 4, "The persons -- those persons who ordered that the depots be opened and that weapons be distributed to the Serbian people knew why they were doing it. It is plain to the Serbian people that they have not been abandoned and that forces exist which take their safety into account." And this is dated as we saw 24th of August, 1991, where it's already saying that those persons who ordered that the depots be opened, weapons be distributed to Serbs -- now you told us yesterday that you'd had an order to distribute weapons, which you'd refused to do. Was that around this period of time? August, September of 1991?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just one correction. In the month of May, 1991, I had a conflict with General Uzelac for this very reason because weapons were requested for units which were not in the JNA. A mobilisation was not announced so my first contact with this issue was actually in May 1991. In the document here, it states clearly that the warehouses are open. Weapons, ammunition, and other military equipment was in the warehouses of the logistics bases. However, the corps commands and their subordinated units had a surplus of weapons, specially when the units pulled out from Slovenia and Croatia, and those weapons were distributed. Counter to regulations and the laws. And they were not issued in the logistics bases but directly from the corps commands. So this can be seen on the basis of this document, which I didn't have before.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So you told us this was in May 1991. That was before any of the conflicts, then?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay. All right. I want to deal --

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you. You can put the document down and I just want to deal, then, with this issue of -- oh, I haven't -- sorry, well, Your Honour I know we used that but as it's already exhibited I don't think we need to re-exhibit it. Thank you. Now, I want to deal, please, then, with this topic of paramilitaries. You've seen these documents. Did you ever have any occasion to come across the actual training by the JNA, by JNA officers in the 5th Corps, of these type of volunteer or paramilitary organisations?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally was not present, and I didn't see the training of such organisations. In Banja Luka there were two firing, training ranges, for smaller infantry weapons. One was in Vrbanja and one in Rakovacke Bare, so the TO units.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The third facility was the Manjaca facility, which was as part of the military academy. I knew it well. I didn't go up there. I didn't have any need to go there, but I know that paramilitary formations went through training there. That I do know.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Can you tell us how you first found out about that?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The officers from my command, naturally, communicated with their colleagues from the corps, from the other units, from the military academy, and this, to each one of us professional officers who had stated the oath was something that bothered all of us. I don't remember all the names right now. It's been a long time ago, but I have taken an oath. So I remain -- I stand by my word.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Now, were you present at any type of conversation in respect of these Manjaca -- the use of the Manjaca training ground, between General Uzelac and anyone else?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was in the office of General Uzelac. We were talking about the problems in the army, the telephone rang, Colonel Bogdan Subotic was calling. The assistant of the chief of the military school for tank training in Banja Luka. He informed him about the training of those paramilitary and volunteer units - I don't know what to call them - in Manjaca. When they finished their conversation, General Uzelac asked me what was Subotic's name? He should go up to Manjaca. He was in charge of the training of those units. That is the first information, official information, that I had from an authorised body that these people were legally trained in Manjaca.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was another occasion, but this was already in May, 1992. So --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm going to come on to that in a moment. I just want to deal with this. First of all, when was this conversation at which you were present, between Subotic and Uzelac?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It may have been, it could have been November 1991, because General Uzelac was the corps commander until the 28th of December, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: When you say "that is the first information, official information, that I had from an authorised body that these people were legally trained in Manjaca," maybe in the translation, did you use the word "legally"?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Manjaca training ground is a legal military facility. It's very large. It was built up over 15 -- a period of 15 years to train tank operators of all types. So if people are trained in that facility, that can only be legally and something that is approved by the authorised military organs.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, you told us that there was -- you were present in May on another occasion, May of 1992, when there was some discussion about this. Where was this discussion taking place, and with whom?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my official notebook, I have written down the date, but I can reproduce it without that. However, if the Court would like me to look at my official notebook, or I can just state that now and then if the Court requests, I can document that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. I think it is better that you use your official notebook for this, although I was going to take events in order. Could you take out your notebook?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the entry in relation to this you will find on, I think -- there is a document as well -- yes. It's I think, Your Honour, it's the 21st of June, I think. I think, Your Honour -- 1st of June.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. That could be the 1st of June.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. If Your Honours goes to page 159, the entry begins on page 158 but the relevant part is on page 159 -- maybe not. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In my official notebook, I have found the date, the 1st of June, 1992, reporting to the commander of the 1st Krajina Corps, General Talic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Is this under "assignments"?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It would be, probably.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. That's right. When the corps commander started to speak, then after that, are assignments, there are six tasks, assignments that he issued. Can I quote them?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Certainly. Yes, if you deal with, I think it's 1, isn't it, and 4?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first task is to arm all soldiers at Manjaca. Task number 4 is the prisoner of war camp at Manjaca, urgent, for approximately 2.500 people.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And was anything said, that you recall, outside your note, in respect of the paramilitaries who were training there?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was stated that all units, all paramilitary formations, have to be removed from the Manjaca training ground. It's written down somewhere.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, we may come back to that because I know that there is a document also from the -- an actual official document that I can't find just at the moment, that deals with that. Now, finally, on this question of paramilitaries, were you in Banja Luka at the beginning of April of 1992?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And do you recall a group of armed men coming into Banja Luka and setting up barricades?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Calling themselves the Serb defence forces, the SOS?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Had you heard of such a group calling itself the SOS before this?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: In what connection?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Serb Defence Forces were formed precisely at that time, and for a brief period, for about two months, I was appointed the chief of the group of officers for cooperation with the UN, with the UNPROFOR forces. 15 UNPROFOR officers came to Banja Luka, and knowing what stupid things and what problems were going on in town at night, there were robberies at the checkpoints, also, and other things, so I discussed with those UNPROFOR officers that they should not move about town at night. They should remain at their hotel, the Hotel Bosna where they were staying and that they shouldn't move around town. So I was concerned about their security and I was also responsible for it. But after that, I was replaced from that duty and then I came back to be the commander of the base. So I didn't really perform that function for more than two months, because I was not appropriate from the political aspect for that -- for that job.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Whose duty was it to deal with these men who had arrived in town and were putting up barricades?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The main responsibility was of the organs of the internal affairs of SUP, the civilian police, and if they were not able to resolve the problem, then they would ask for assistance from the military police or the corps units to remove those people to resolve the problem, to protect the people and to make sure that normal life was restored. However, this was never done. These White Eagles, they went from Banja Luka, someone went away from Banja Luka, but however these problems continued. There were arrests of people, robberies and so on. And I can say they legally [as interpreted], openly, sold weapons in the streets of Banja Luka in front of the barracks to people, to passers-by.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Pause please, Colonel Selak, can I just remind you because I think there was a problem with the translation, they didn't catch what you said -- not to go too quickly. You say these "White Eagles" --

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you call these people White Eagles? Are you referring to the people in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were mixed. The people didn't know exactly who they were. I'm talking about what's going on in Banja Luka, Red Berets, White Eagles, formations of Lieutenant Milankovic. So these were all these groups that went all throughout Bosanska Krajina. They were in Banja Luka and people in the town mixed them all up. You never officially knew who was who.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Korner we need to correct something as well because here on the transcript, I see that, "And I can say they legally, openly sold weapons in the streets of Banja Luka." Did you say "legally" or "illegally"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Legally. It's a mistake. Openly, without authorisation, in front of the Kozara barracks, there was a place where people could buy weapons. So it's not legally, they simply got their hands on weapons in an unauthorized way. They had a surplus of weapons and they were selling them openly in the street.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think what you meant was in a sense of they were selling illegally but were being allowed to do it openly, as you just explained. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Illegally, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. What I'm just concerned with, I think, is it right? Through the period that you remained in Banja Luka, other paramilitary groups, calling themselves White Eagles or whatever, came in, I'm just concentrating on the people calling themselves the Serbian Defence Forces. You told us it was the civilian authorities' duty to remove them, and if they didn't, couldn't do it themselves, then to seek the assistance of the army. Who was the person who -- or persons who should have been directing the police to remove these people from the streets of Banja Luka, which authorities?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all the Crisis Staff of Banja Luka, the President of the Banja Luka municipality, the chief of the Public Security Services or SUP Banja Luka, and the military, General Talic also had to have intervened and to have demanded that this be resolved, and in case this was necessary, to provide assistance to the MUP in order to resolve this situation.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You say the Crisis Staff. By that, do you mean the Crisis Staff that had been set up in response to that situation?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Crisis Staff in Banja Luka already existed in 1991 [as interpreted], and based on Crisis Staffs being formed throughout Bosanska Krajina. So it went by municipalities, each one had their own Crisis Staff. And it took over the authority of the assembly and worked on behalf of the assembly. So it was responsible for the entire life in the whole municipality.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Sorry, Colonel Selak, it may be a long time ago and you're right that in each municipality, Crisis Staffs were set up at different times, but in 1991, there was no Crisis Staff, official Crisis Staff, set up in Banja Luka, was there? It came in in 1992.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think it's a translation error. He said 1992, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Oh, did he?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think it's important, Your Honour, that is something -- on dates, the interpreters should say if they have had made a mistake state straight away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I agree with you. I take it from what Mr. Ackerman said having the assistance of Ms. Jevtovic that he did say 1992, but it needed to be corrected in any case because the transcript that we have here says 1991. So...

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That's all right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Colonel Selak, that's why, it's not your fault, I know because we ask you questions and you're giving us answers if you could try and slow down in your answer so the interpreters could keep up. Thank you. Right.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you. It's a professional deformity.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. I want to move now, please, to the events through your diary, and then when we get to, deal with the topic of dismissals in the JNA and how it affected you. I would like you, please, first of all, because your diary -- I'm sorry, I apologise. I keep calling it your diary, your notebook begins in December of 1991. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The 19th of December, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, I would like you, please, just before we do that, to have a look at a document that relates to you and a number of other people, before the 19th of December. Could you be handed, please, 4.1718. It's a document dated the 3rd of December, 1991. It's from the 5th Corps. And effectively, it's I think a recommendation for awards to be given. And do we see that under the order of the peoples army with laurel wreath, you and indeed your assistant commander, Tepsic, were supposed to be awarded this particular order?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What kind of an order was it? It says above that -- well, I should perhaps have read the first bit, "For competence and courage in command and control of units during wartime assignments." Is that effectively, that's what it was for?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Did you ever get that award as it turned out?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes -- no, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Was any explanation given to you why you weren't being given this award?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I was not given any explanation. I did not even know about this document. This surprised me very much. The logistics base was carrying out its tasks correctly and the inspections always found the state of affairs there to be excellent, and that is probably the basis for this, but it was a political decision that was probably made elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Do you know whether -- I think it's Colonel Tepsic got his award?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 22nd of December, I was at the army hall. That was the holiday, the JNA day, that was always celebrated. So that is when these awards were carried out too but I don't know who all the persons who got them were. There were many people present there. I did not know that I had even been a candidate. So at that time I wasn't even hoping for any such thing. Let's put it that way.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. You can put that document away.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, could that be made, please, Exhibit P1575?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, you've already explained to the Court what this work, official notebook, consisted of, and how you compiled it. On the 20th of December.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, at page 3.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Is there an entry under political and moral guidance, which reads, "The SFRY order communicated to the troops"? Is that the entry there that you have --

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I have the assistant for morale in my command, Major Pavlovic. He said at the meeting of the organs of my command that an order of the Presidency of the SFRY addressed to all the units was read out. This was something that had to do with --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Don't worry about what the order was because I'm not -- unless you think it's particularly important.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All I'm interested in is this: Was that a routine procedure that the political instructions would be communicated to the troops?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was not addressed to the units. It was addressed to the organs of my command. They were the ones who were told. They were the one who is were supposed to be made aware of these orders, and he only familiarised us, that is to say my subordinates and myself with these orders.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay. In that case, I think it may be the way it's translated. So what you're saying is you, the officers, would be told what the orders were from the Presidency?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please. I'm quoting this. This is a meeting with --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please read slower? The interpreters cannot keep up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Colonel, the interpreters are finding it difficult to catch up with your speed, with the speed with which you're talking. So if you could slow down, please, you would be helping them. And they need that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Can you tell us very simply in one sentence: What does this entry mean?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This note of mine says that the officers of the command were made aware of the order of the Presidency of the SFRY.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And is that something that would happen on a regular basis?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Then could you move to the 26th of December? At that stage, were you in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And if you find, please, under 8, you noted down, General Vidovic?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: At that stage, 26th of December, had General Vidovic taken over command of the 5th Corps?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. General Vukovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Somebody different. Who was General Vidovic?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Vidovic was assistant commander of the 1st military district in Belgrade for political affairs and morale.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And he stated there, he talked about the international recognition of the republics of Slovenia and Croatia. And then said this: "Yugoslavia will survive, part of Bosnia-Herzegovina with Yugoslavia? The Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Serbian Krajinas and others will be part of the new Yugoslavia." Is that what you wrote down?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is a direct quote.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And what nationality was General Vidovic?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Serb.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What was your reaction when you heard what he was saying there?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I managed to write down all the issues that were presented at this meeting. I was a bit upset by all of this but I had to remain silent and be wise.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And it may seem obvious but why were you a bit upset?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I was upset how come there could be a Serb Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina in Yugoslavia. I personally was in favour of Yugoslavia, but a Yugoslavia of all its peoples, and here it says: "The Serb Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina," and that surprised me and it astounded me actually. Also, reference is made to the Serb Krajinas here. These are the Krajinas from Croatia. As a professional officer, it was clear to me how this would come about, and how efforts would be made in order to have this objective achieved.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And at that stage, if you can, taking yourself back to December, 1991, how did you think this was to be achieved?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: 1991? This option, and this solution to the political crisis in the territory of the former Yugoslavia, could be carried out only by way of war, because it is certain that the Muslim people, rather the Bosniak people and the Croat people in Bosnia-Herzegovina would not allow this kind of a political settlement, and this leads to war.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Finishing off the entries for this date, then, please, could you find under 10 what a General Crmaric said? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's a wrong spelling of the name.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Crmaric. That is my direct superior.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And that I think is spelled C-r-m-a-r-i-c?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: C-r-m.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. He is giving you instructions there, or instructs to be given -- do not issue weapons to TO for units not approved by the federal national Defence secretariat. Now, we've already had a look at a number of documents that went on you -- but to your knowledge, was the corps later given permission to hand out arms outside those approved units?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was told verbally at a meeting at the corps commander's office that the corps had received approval from the federal secretariat for national defence in terms of the following: That within their own area of responsibility, they could issue arms and equipment to others. Of course, of course, within the legal framework of the mobilisation of units. That is the way I understood it, that it would be done within the legal framework, namely that mobilisation would be officially declared, in terms of a particular wartime unit, or Territorial Defence. On that basis, General Uzelac, the commander of the corps in general, could issue an order to me to issue weapons to that kind of a unit.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And who told you verbally that the corps had been given permission to issue weapons outside approved units?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I attended meetings of the corps command regularly in General Uzelac's office where all other questions were looked at as well. Those related to combat readiness and the like, within the corps, and I don't know who provided this information.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Sorry, I should have -- can I just go back -- I forgot to ask you about General Vidovic. Was he a senior officer in the JNA?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And so this was him giving the political objective to subordinates, was it?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I beg your pardon, he is presenting the positions of the general staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, previously he said that he was assistant commander of the 1st military district in Belgrade for political affairs and morale.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What I'm trying to establish is that that is a senior position.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, yes, yes, a very senior position.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And then finally, I think, on this meeting of the 26th of December, could you find a section that says, "Commander"? It's page 9 of our translation.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Commander," yes, commander of the 1st military district, Colonel General Spirkovski.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Was he the most senior officer presents at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Who in some ways was echoing what General Vidovic had said, "With the exception of just a few countries, the whole world is eager to see the SFRY disintegrate with the World War II axis powers leading the pack and European countries making it possible." Now, what nationality was the most senior officer there?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Macedonian.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The -- well, I thought -- ethnicity? You say Macedonian. Was that a separate ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Orthodox religion.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. He sort of harks back to World War II, axis powers. Was that a theme that occurred more than once during the period leading to the conflict, the World War II events?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They mentioned the situation that existed in the Second World War and the objection made to Germany was that they stood on the side of Croatia and the Bosniak people in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and that that is what they expected of Germany, and the so-called axis powers, but they were specifically speaking about Germany and my comment follows.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And then the next, "Everything being done in Yugoslavia has been prepared for many years." Is that what he said?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, those are his words. Please, this is a quotation. Your Honours, these are sentences that are written that way. Also, a handwriting expert can check this out.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's all right. There is no -- it's all right, Colonel. Nobody is suggesting it's a forgery. I just want to know whether it was your comments or what he said. What was he referring to there, do you know?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The meaning of this was, according to the words of the commander and of the other officers, the generals, who spoke, was that it was held against the west that they were trying to topple communism in Yugoslavia and that is why the Second World War was mentioned, in that context.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. We can leave that entry.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour the next entry I want to look at is quite a lengthy one so perhaps it can be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So we'll have a break of 25 minutes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Where is the witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry, he was kept out just for one second. Literally. Your Honour, I want to make an application to exceed a page limit for a motion. We are reapplying for the witness summons for Mr. Randal, in the light of the Appeals Chamber's decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Are you applying also for summons to be issued against the other journalist as well?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, we are going to be explaining this, because we find the Appeals Chamber's ruling on this somewhat extraordinary --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It would be very interesting if the two journalists are sought to be brought over to give evidence. And both of them refused to.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, as Your Honour saw and Your Honour has taken the point this is the most circular decision I've ever seen. Would we are going to reapply but I would like to exceed the ten page limit, 20 pages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Just for formality. Granted. Where is the witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: He's being brought in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We will be continuing with this note?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, we are going to go through that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you think you will finish with the witness today?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. But I will finish tomorrow definitely, and I'll finish before the end of tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. And you will be a position to start your cross tomorrow, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, I just discussed that Mr. Ms. Korner. I'll be in a position to start but maybe not finish tomorrow. I may want to carry over to -- even adjourn early tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That would suit me fine because I needs to be at the airport at 3.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. Then I think we'll accommodate you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But the witness will have to be informed that he will be staying.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We anticipated that and we informed him about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Colonel, we are continuing.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Colonel, can we now move to your entry for the 1st of January, 1992?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: For our purposes, Your Honour, it begins at page 15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And was this you on the 1st of January reporting to the commander of the 5th Corps?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And can you now turn, please, to the entry that is headed, "Tasks of the 5th Corps commander," which is at our page 17?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And if you just remind us again so that I don't make the mistake, who was the commander of the 5th Corps in January?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Vukovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And is this -- where you've got this headed of the tasks of the 5th Corps commander, is this him telling what you is expected?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The corps commander talks here. The tasks of the corps commander, which he is transferring to us, his subordinates.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. All right. We see 1, the tasks from the federal secretariat of national Defence. And so is he relaying to you, his officers, the tasks that had been set by the federal secretariat?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And then we see that the problem they say can be solved by deploying UN forces?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And then, under 2, "The position of the JNA and SFRY Presidency is the problem must be solved in a peaceful manner with UN forces but with separating forces." And here, is this in relation to the conflict in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And this is more about what the solution would be. And then can we come down to the reasoning that the supreme staff is committed to, "The JNA had two tasks: To protect the Serbs in" -- and you've written -- RH, from genocide. Is that the Republika Hvratska, Croatia?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Were you surprised that apparently the JNA's view was that the only people who should be protected were the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was a surprise to me. I didn't believe this information completely. It wasn't logical.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: "And then to withdraw the JNA troops and families of servicemen and the military equipment from Croatia." And then it goes on again, "Serbian-populated areas continue to be protected against genocide. This task is in progress and has been carried out well so far." What was your understanding of the role of the JNA in respect of protection?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understood this when earlier General Vidovic said that Yugoslavia would survive, that Serbian Krajinas and the Serb Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina were in Yugoslavia, that the JNA was that force that would separate the Serbian Krajina from Croatia and join it to Yugoslavia. That was my understanding of this information.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Before these remarks were made by these senior officers, was your understanding of the JNA that it should protect one nationality only? The role of the JNA, I should say.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't. I understood it as the army of all the ethnic groups, all the peoples, and as such, I made -- gave my oath, and I fought for that with full conviction.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And then it goes on, the commander went on to say that, later, "Our actions must be free from --" I'm sorry, yes, could you read that sentence that begins, "Our actions"?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The present moment --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's the next sentence.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think there is an error in the translation. That's why I'm asking that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I understood that straight away.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please repeat the question?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could you just read, Colonel Selak, you've read -- you've seen the sentence which begins, "The present moment." Could you read the next sentence after that?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. "Everything that we do must be beyond any party or political nuance, without any option for any party but with all of those who wish for Yugoslavia."

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What did you understand that the general was saying in this sentence?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is how I understood it, that they wanted Yugoslavia to survive but within the new borders, the way it was delineated in the military and political circles. So Yugoslavia, with Serbia, Montenegro, Macedonia, the Serb Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the Serb Krajina, and that was and is now part of the territory of the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Can we then move, please, to your heading, "Commentary on reports"? It's our page 18. The commentary on reports that -- your headline, what does that mean? Who was giving a commentary?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a commentary on reports. That's what it says in my notebook, and this is still the commander, the commander of the 5th Corps who is speaking.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. And then he -- under the 5th Corps tasks, he talks about the bridgehead at the Sava River, securing the line, and expand this into the area populated by Serbs, in order to prevent the Croatian army from committing genocide against Serbian population. Does it read, "Secure a passage for the area populated by Serbs"?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And then it deals with the UN forces. Now, could you read, please, the next paragraph -- or the next bit, which starts, "The objective"?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. "The objective could be formulated in the following way: Up to 20.000 Croatian soldiers to be free to engage in Srem, Lika, and Kordun and to prevent Croatian nationalism and Ustasha ideas from spreading in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina populated by Croats. To prevent the alliance of Croatian and Muslim nationalists so that peoples of Bosnia and Herzegovina can express their wish as to what kind of a state they desire to live in."

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The 20.000 troops or Croatian troops, what was being said there? Don't read it again. Just tell us what the effect of what the commander was saying there is. What should happen in respect of 20.000 troops?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understood it to mean that the units of the 5th Corps, with their engagement in the front, should link those or engage those 20.000 Croat soldiers so that they are not free to commit genocide against the Serb population.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay. Then can we move, please, next further on in your diary, in your workbook, to the 6th of January? Just very briefly. Was -- we can see that virtually the same words about the JNA protecting Serbs from genocide, et cetera, are repeated. Was that you briefing your officers on what had been said by the commander?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. On the 6th of January, I had a meeting with my subordinate bodies, and as commander, I regularly informed them and conveyed to them information that I received from the 5th Corps commander. I have just quoted all the information that we went through earlier.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: And I also quoted the tasks assigned to my command, to my unit. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Now, part of what the commander had told you and which you passed on to your officers under your command could be said to be a political goal. Was it mandatory that those goals were followed by the officers under the commands of the generals?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. If anybody had any dilemmas or something wasn't clear, he should ask at the meeting, and additional information should have been given to them. A person was not supposed to leave a meeting with anything that was not clear.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Now, on that note, it's a slightly earlier document but it deals with the same topic, could you be shown, please, a document 42159. It's a document dated the 10th of December, 1991. And it comes, I think, from the federal secretariat for national defence. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: He's actually addressed -- this particular version that we've acquired is addressed to the 9th Corps commander and it's copy number 25, apparently, but would this document have been sent to the commanders of all the corps?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And it's signed and stamped, I think, for somebody standing in for a General Major Polic?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And he was who?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what his duties were. I heard about General Polic. He was in the general staff of the armed forces of the SFRY. I don't know where he is now but he did have the right to sign and stamp on behalf of the general staff, and it states here that an authorised person signed this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. All right. And is it right that in handwriting, it says that "This is all people's defence, use in the elaboration of coming activities and send units, orders to units, informing them of tasks," or something like that anyhow?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And the deadline was given, the 20th of December, 1991, for that to be done, and it is stated clearly in the Cyrillic script.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, you told us about your meeting in Belgrade that you had on the 20th of December, and where the various things were communicated to you, and then on the 26th of December. Could you look, please -- there is a description of the -- I'm sorry, first of all, the headnote, "Directive on the use of the armed forces for the preparation and performance of combat operations in the forthcoming period." And then there is a description of the background and the events. Could you look, please, at paragraph with the roman numeral II?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: "Our armed forces are entering a new period of exceptional significance for accomplishing the ultimate aims of the war." And then "protection of the Serbian people -- of the Serbian population." In the original, is that circled, those words?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't know if Ms. Korner knows the answer. Was this -- this circling and underlining and all of this done by people at the OTP or did the document acquire -- was it acquired in this form?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, as far as I know, and I'll check I'll have to get the original from the evidence unit, but this was done -- this is on the original copy but I will check that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, please do, Ms. Korner, and let us know. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And then, "Protection of the Serbian population, a peaceful resolution of the Yugoslav crisis and the creation of conditions in which Yugoslavia may be preserved." And then it sets out tasks and could we look at paragraph number 6 of tasks?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: "In all zones of combat operations, place under the command of the most senior JNA officers all units of the JNA and TO as well as volunteer units which agree to be subordinate to that command and wear JNA and TO insignia. Consider all other armed formations paramilitaries, disarm them and remove them from the BD zone."

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Combat operations, "borbena dejstva," BD.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Now, you've had a chance -- I don't want to go through any more of the document but you've had a chance to read it I think before. To your recollection -- we saw that you were being briefed on instructions from the secretariat of national defence. Were these the instructions that were being read to you?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Instructions were not read to me but at the meeting, at the corps commanders, this was discussed and the unit commanders and all of those subordinated persons who were present at the meeting had to write this down in their official notebooks and this was later an official document for command and control and for ongoing duties.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. You can put that document away there but could that be made P1576, please? And now can we move, please n your work notebook to the 9th of January, our page 28, but the part that I just want to ask you about is our page -- our page 30. Can you find the entry under the third fuel depot. Have you written, "Some of the troops --" well, I'm sorry. Can you read that sentence which begins, "Some of the troops," and it's to do with ethnic -- I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 9th, just one moment, please. Yes. Yes. There are two. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: There is a paragraph 3, third fuel depot.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes. I found it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can you just read the entry that begins, "Some of the troops"?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Some of unemployed letting people go home."

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Unemployed" -- I don't have "some of the troops." Maybe it's a mistake. Oh, yes, yes, yes. "Some of the troops working because of ethnic grounds."

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And what did you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the reporting of commanders who are subordinated to me. So this third fuel depot and other fuels was in Jajce. The commander the warehouse, Major Vojo Musunski from Macedonia, reports to me, and from his I noted down that some of the troops were working because of ethnic grounds. So these are some troops in our -- in his unit, who are already divided along ethnic lines. And this is what he talked about.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Had that happened before the conflict broke out in Croatia, that troops of different ethnicities grouped themselves together?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Before the war in Croatia, soldiers, young men of 18, socialised according to their preferences. They did socialise, of course, if they happened to be from the same area. For example, Macedonia and socialised with Macedonians because of their common habits. But along ethnic lines, it was something that was problematic and it wasn't really permitted.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. And then can you move, then, please, to the 16th of January? Page 40 for us.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We see an entry under the introduction that relates apparently to an armoured battalion from Pancevo?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can you just tell us where was that? Where did this battalion come from?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
