utterances.text: The armoured battalion was from Pancevo, Serbia. And it was resubordinated to the units that fought against the Croat forces in Kupres and at Lake Plitvice in Croatia. The commander of this group was Colonel Vitomir Grujic who was serving in Banja Luka at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And on this point of units coming from Serbia to fight, could you find, please, under your paragraph 2, and it's at our page 42, a part dealing with those units from Serbia? It starts, "Reception of the units from Serbia."

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I remember that. Yes. I've found it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We can see it talks about their lack of material and providing them with equipment. To try and shorten this, was the fact there that these people were arriving without proper equipment, you had to provide it for them, or your logistics unit, and then when they left the front line, in other words they deserted, they took this equipment with them?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I give a broader explanation regarding this particular case?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If you can keep it quite short.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in a few sentences.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Yes.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The mechanised brigade from Loznica, Serbia, passed through Banja Luka during those days. Behind the vehicles of the brigade was a column of over 100 trucks with trailers that were completely empty. The brigade was marching towards Croatia, towards Karlovac. A few days later, after they had carried out combat operations in Croatia, the brigade sustained major losses, left the positions in Croatia, and returned with empty trucks to Serbia. Among the citizens of Banja Luka, this caused bitterness, this kind of behaviour did. But this is not the only case of such behaviour of these units that came, not only to fight but also to loot the property of the population that lived there.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. We'll see an entry relating to that. But what was the significance that they returned with empty trucks to Serbia?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The significance is that they had planned to have war booty. I mean, I'm calling it the spoils of war under quotation marks because it's sheer looting. There is no logic involved in this. Why would trucks go? Because for all logistics purposes, there was this logistics base that I had headed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. I understand, Colonel Selak. What you're saying is they brought empty trucks to collect war booty, but in actual fact they didn't get any?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. So it was the fact that these people were trying to collect war booty that was causing the resentment?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And indeed can we look finally on this entry and we'll move forward to the next month to your conclusion, our page 43? Paragraph 3 of your conclusion, "The war booty was never entered in the books and my personal opinion is that this matter should be looked into by the military organisations."

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The war booty, let me call it that way rather than plunder, I mean I'm talking about ammunition, about weapons, fuel, medicine. The official organs at the logistics base had to have a look to record everything, to register it properly in the books, and also they should keep whatever is in good condition and get rid of whatever was in improper condition. Unfortunately, the corps units never handed in a single bullet, to my organs.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: They themselves disposed of this.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Colonel Selak, you were actually living in Banja Luka at this period of time. What was the behaviour of these returning soldiers like when they passed through Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The units that marched through Banja Luka -- actually these soldiers were on trucks. They did not take any breaks in the area of Banja Luka itself. So there were no contacts with these soldiers, with the officers. But the people threw stones at them.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Let's move on. Thank you. Can we look, please, at the 24th of February?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Our page 66, Your Honour, although it's actually at page 68 that I want to look at.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could you find, Colonel Selak, your entry for that date, the 24th, under the second ammunition depot section?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a department of the fuel depot in Donji Vakuf, Bosnia-Herzegovina,

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Ammunition depot, interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And what have you recorded under there?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I called the commander of this depot, Lieutenant Savic, to come and report to me.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. I think there may be a problem with interpretation. All I want -- it's my fault for using the word "recorded." What did you write immediately underneath the words, "Second ammunition depot section"?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Serb Municipality of Donji Vakuf proclaimed."

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Was that reported to you by one of your officers?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's just what I wanted to say. Lieutenant Savic was commander of that depot.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. When you heard this news, what was your reaction to the news that a Serbian municipality had been declared in Donji Vakuf?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was in the municipality of Donji Vakuf very often. I knew the situation in the municipality. And this surprised me very much. However, this is also the result of the following: The records of the Territorial Defence unit were taken away by the SDS, and weapons were received by Serb military conscripts only.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: How did you find out about that?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is what the President of the municipality told me, Kemal Terzic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And then can we just deal with one further entry for that page? It appears that near a sawmill on the road to Slatina, roadblocks had been set up. Was that anything to do with the takeover of the municipality -- or the declaration of the Serbian municipality, or was that a separate incident?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is not separate from the takeover of the municipality or the declaration of the Serbian municipality. A roadblock was put so that vehicles could not pass. I believe that this was done out of fear, in order to keep the population safe, that is. However, the police reacted and the roadblock was removed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And can you remember, I mean, who had set up the roadblock? Was is the Serbs or the Bosniaks, the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that it was the Bosniaks, the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Because --

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that the ethnic pattern was more or less the same in this municipality. There were only 4 per cent Croats and the Serbs and Muslims were more or less there in the same numbers.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay. Can we move from there quite substantially on in your notebook, please, just to note, please, this is the 11th of March, page 84, and the entry at page 85? Was this entry concerned --

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a minute, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have the 12th of March. Yes, yes, do I have something on the 11th of March, yes, that's right, all right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: There is a discussion with the liaison group for cooperation in logistics with the UN peacekeeping force. Was that at the time that you were appointed the liaison officer with the UN peacekeeping forces?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I was head of that group.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And can you just tell us how long did you remain the officer in charge of liaison?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I took over that duty sometime in the beginning of the month of February, and I handed it over towards the end of March. So it was less than two months altogether.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Do you know why you had to relinquish that position?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a meeting at President Radic's. Mr. Brdjanin also attended the meeting. What was discussed was the deployment of officers, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. or rather UN forces, in the area of Banja Luka. President Radic offered the Palace Hotel for accommodating these officers, and the building of the retirees' home on the banks of the Vrbas River, which had not been completed yet. In order to cover the expenses for using these facilities, they asked for 2 million dollars, U.S. dollars. The officers of the UN forces did not wish to accept that. It was not logical either. I was also opposed to that. I suggested that they be accommodated at the Mladjan Stojanovic barracks where the military academy used to be, or the so-called Rakovacke Bare which is where Territorial Defence units were put up. After that, there was a clash. This position of mine was resented, and I was replaced from that particular duty.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What was Mr. Brdjanin's attitude on this?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot recall his words, but they were in favour of the Hotel Palace and the retirees' home. This position of theirs was logical to me because they wanted these facilities to be paid for well so this would improve their finances, but there was no logic in terms of this from a military point of view. The UN officers insisted that they should be close to their soldiers, which is only logical.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Was anybody else from your corps there, any senior officers? Or was it just you, the UN officers, Mr. Radic and Mr. Brdjanin?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember who else was there. There were other persons there. This was at the Office of the President of the municipality. There were several of us there. I did not write down, though, who all the persons present were. So I cannot remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. How long after that were you removed?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was the 11th of March, and by the end of March, I had been removed. I have a document on my replacement. I have it here in my bag. So I was returned to my duty as head of the logistics base at Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And how do you know that it had anything to do with the fact that you were opposed to what Mr. Brdjanin and Mr. Radic wanted, namely that, you know, the UN should pay a couple of million dollars for their accommodation?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew President Radic from before, and after this, President Radic really held this against me, and he said to me that Banja Luka had lost 2 million dollars because of my point of view. It was my own assessment that this was one of the reasons why I was replaced -- I say one of the reasons. Allow me to note another thing: That the battalion of the logistics forces of the UN, after that, was stationed in Pancevo, near Belgrade. The security centre in Pancevo was moved out and the battalion of the logistics forces of the UN moved in.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. I see. I'm sorry, I thought it was -- can I stick for a moment with the question of your removal? Would President Radic have had influence with your command to have you removed?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: President Radic personally could not have done that. He presented his point of view. He presented this information as to what had happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I understand that. You've explained that a politician couldn't order the removal or order a change of duty. But would a politician in that position be listened to in respect of the views and therefore the military would then take a decision based on those views?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have information that the command of the Banja Luka Corps, before the group for cooperation with the UN was set up, had suggested that Colonel Vaso Tepsic be head of this group, instead of me.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can I stop you for a moment, Colonel Selak? Is this going to be an answer to my question? Because the question was quite straightforward. It is: Would a politician, leader of a municipality, have influence, be listened to, in respect of his views so that the military would take a decision based on those views?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Objectively speaking, no, but he had a greater influence in the military, in the corps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, let me try and help a little bit. Ms. Korner -- Colonel, Ms. Korner pointed out to you that in general terms, a politician would never be in a position to directly sack or -- a military officer, or move him from one position to another.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: However --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: However, her next point was: Would the politician, however, be able to bear influence on the military authorities to do what the politician wouldn't be able to do? In other words, to sack or to move the military officer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you for that. Thank you very much, Your Honour. All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, Colonel, there is one other person I wanted to ask you about in that entry.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, before we move on, otherwise I will forget, we've got the original of this document Mr. Ackerman asked about from the evidence unit, and it's the -- the underlining has clearly been done by them, so it's not a photocopy that has been marked by us. I don't know if Mr. Ackerman wants to have a look at the original.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the Presiding Judge, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's with regard to. That's are regard to P1576, correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: When she says the underlining has clear by been done by them, who is it she is speaking of, do you know?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, when I say "them," it's not been underlined by a lawyer in the reading of this document. This is how the document was acquired by the institution. So I can't say who underlined it, but it wasn't us. "Us" being the OTP.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Can I be reminded of the exhibit number? I want to look at something for just a second.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I found it. I found it. Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Let's move forward.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we now look, please, at another document, following through the progression of things.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Because, I'm going to move from there until another date in April. Could you be handed, please, what was Exhibit 165 in the Tadic case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think we saw that yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I don't think so, Your Honour. It's date -- a document dated the 8th of April, headed, "2nd Military District command." The only Tadic exhibits I looked at I think were all the various diagrams.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Disclosure number?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No disclosure number. It was attached -- it may have been disclosed -- it could have been disclosed before but it was actually attached to the Tadic transcript. If you've got the Tadic transcript with the bundle of exhibits, it was attached to that. We can put the English versions -- the English version is on the ELMO, in any event.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Colonel Selak, this is addressed, it's from the 2nd Military District command, addressed to the 5th and other commands plus the logistic base commands. Did you see this order from commander General Kukanjac at the time? In other words in April, 1992?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And it's effectively, if we can summarise it, it's moving, relocating, the units and institution on the territory of the -- I think the RS Krajina, which is the Croatian Krajina, is it not?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And just very briefly, what was this document -- what was the purpose of this document?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The units of the 2nd army or rather the 5th Corps in Banja Luka that were stationed in Croatia had to withdraw from the areas where the UN units would be deployed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did this have any practical effect?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: As far as you -- and what was that?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a meeting of the corps commanders and we were entrusted with the following task: The units of the JNA and the TO that remained in Slavonia were supposed to provide logistics to the units of the 2nd Military District in Sarajevo. And thereby, the 5th Corps in Banja Luka and also the logistics base in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And did they go to Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The units did not go to Sarajevo. They remained in other areas, and we gave them logistic support.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you. All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, that better have a new exhibit number. 1577.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, can we look, please, at your workbook, your official notebook, for the 9th of April, the following day? Did you have a meeting with the President of the Donji Vakuf of the municipal assembly?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Was this -- I don't know, had by that stage a Serbian assembly been declared or was this still the official, proper assembly president?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Kemal Terzic was the official president of the municipal assembly of Donji Vakuf at that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And was this -- you've told us that one of your duties and the duties of the army generally was to cooperate and maintain relationships with the political leaders, the local ones. Was this a regular visit?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was my duty to regularly visit the organs of authority in the municipality, the President of the municipality, the chief of the SUP and others, so that was my obligation, and on the 9th of April, I was visiting the President of Donji Vakuf.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And he was telling you, was he, about the Muslims standing guard, that there weren't any barricades, that and there were checks going on but that there were also incidents? What did he want you to do, if anything, Mr. Terzic?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: From my notebook, where I wrote down about that meeting, I can see that the President informed me about the political and security situation in the municipality. He also mentioned the barricades, their removal, the guards, that there was shooting.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, can I stop you, Colonel Selak? He was giving you a report of what happened. Did he want you to do anything about it?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And what was that?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He asked for the army to intervene, to resolve that, to help with the settlement of the security situation in his municipality.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: In normal circumstances, if a president of a municipality made such a request, would the army assist?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In normal circumstances, the police should have intervened and only if the police did not have enough forces, then they should have asked for help from the authorised bodies of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. And if then they couldn't resolve it either, then the army would have to get involved in the resolution of the situation. I personally at that time was not able to help him, but I did tell him that I would come with Colonel Galic, the commander of the 30th Division, to see what could be done regarding this matter.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. And we'll see that you -- there was such a meeting a little later. I'm very sorry, can I just go back, please, to an entry in your diary for the 11th of March. There was one person I meant to ask you about. Page 84 of Your Honours' bundle.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: There is an entry, I can never do this one, Sasa the year of 1990?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I don't think I'm particularly interested in what it's about. There is a name there, Miroslav Majstorovic, Lieutenant Colonel, security organ?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Lieutenant Colonel.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. What did I say? Who was he? I can see he was security organs. But what was the meeting there about?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Lieutenant Colonel in charge of security was from the operative group, from Croatia. I don't know why I noted down his name here, and his telephone number. It was probably something about personnel, about his assignment, and about eight officers were with him and three civilians, who came. I believe that later, they went to the 30th Partisan division.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. All I want to know is: Do you know what he did during the period of the conflict between May and August of 1992? Do you know where he was?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that he was in the 30th Partisan Division but I'm not sure, because based on this information, all the officers who came to that area were assigned to different duties. I didn't have time to really have so much contact with them.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. So you didn't hear of him in particular as to where he was during that period? If you didn't -- I don't think you did say so.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. I'm sorry to go back. I just wanted to ask about that. Now, still sticking to that, can we look -- this is the same day, the 9th of April. Did you also pay a visit to Jajce?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, I don't -- because we are not dealing with the events in Jajce at all in this case, but there, do you record that a Crisis Staff had been established?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, this is page 90, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Which contained representatives of each of the ethnic groups?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were three representing each of the ethnic groups; three Croats, three Bosniaks, and three Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And had this been set up I'm just summarising - it's in the entry so we all understand it - because there had been an incident involving a bus where people had been killed by a -- I think a Croat police officer? We can see a list at the end of your entry of people -- soldiers killed.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: When the murder of these soldiers occurred, the bus was going from Banja Luka to Bugojno. So when this soldier was killed, the seven soldiers were killed, I went and I demanded that this be investigated urgently, and that information be conveyed about the situation in Jajce. Allow me to explain. At the Barevo checkpoint --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, Colonel Selak, because we are not dealing with Jajce. We just wanted so if anybody looked at that entry we would understand what it meant. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. Could you move, please, now to the 13th of April. And there are a number of entries, I think that you made there. Our page 95.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, is the beginning -- is the first entry there, there is a meeting with the base command organs?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I only want to ask you about an entry, it's our page 94, but I think it's been written at the top -- the bottom of that page, where you've written the name Kupresanin and some numbers.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. These are the telephone numbers of Mr. Kupresanin at that time, and I noted that down.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can you remember why that was?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Kupresanin called me on the telephone. He had a problem with fuel for agricultural machinery in the municipality of Srbac, and he asked me to provide one cistern of fuel for agricultural works to be carried Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. out, and that he would then later either return that to me or pay for it. So I issued an order for the fuel to be given, and at that point, we exchanged our telephone numbers. But the fuel was never returned or paid for. But that is not the most important thing here.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. The reason I'm asking you about that is this: That -- did it happen from time to time, or regularly, that politicians, leaders, would speak to you about supplies?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Supplies of material were discussed, which was located in the territory of the municipalities and which were used by the army. There was never any discussion about military materiel in military warehouses. They knew that they should not ask me about that, and really, they did not ask me about that. But I --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think you misunderstand. What you're saying here is Mr. Kupresanin asking you for fuel for Srbac which I think is where he came from. What I want to know is: Were there other requests from other politicians --

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, could we suspend the sitting for a few minutes, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Certainly. Does Your Honour wish to take the break now and then we can come back?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We could do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And come back at --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Colonel Selak, could you now find in your diary, still for the 13th of April, an official interview with a Captain Redzo Trako?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Our page 95. Now, was it part of your duties to deal with the disciplinary aspect of officers within your command?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was my duty.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, this Captain First Class, what nationality was he? What ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Bosniak.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And he was being interviewed that day about his attitude towards the JNA and the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And did you then make a note of some of the things that he was saying?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I wrote down in my official notebook what he said.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: He told you that for him, the army he loved is dying, and then he gave -- said this: "The attitude of the organs of the SOS in Banja Luka towards the JNA, a rifle, a beard, a bottle of brandy, wanting to check military vehicles to see what is being transported." What was his complaint there about the SOS?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: He complained about the conduct of the Serb Defence forces around town, that they carried weapons, that they were growing beards, and beards associate people with Chetniks, that they were under the influence of alcohol, and that this was something that bothered him, and that those people wanted to have -- wanted to control military vehicles. They wanted to check what was being driven in those vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And what was his view about what the JNA should have been doing?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: He also made an oath to the Yugoslav People's Army. He came out stating that he respected the laws of that army, and that what was happening now was not that army.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yeah. What did he think, and specifically, that the JNA should have been doing in respect of the behaviour of the SOS forces?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: He wanted this to be resolved so that life could return to normal in the town of Banja Luka. That was the essence of what he said. He provided also some specific information about the conduct of some other people.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This conversation was attended by --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. I'm sorry, Colonel Selak, I'm going to deal with each of the things he said in turn. In the next part of your entry, there is a reference to Vojo Kupresanin calling a Captain First Class Radan from Mrkonjic Grad. What's that referring to?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know that he had this information or where he got it from. This was on the 13th of April, that he had a conversation with Mr. Kupresanin and this person Captain First Class Bulajic. I wasn't interested in the topic of their conversation, and I didn't discuss it any further.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But can you -- I know it's a long time ago. Can you remember what his complaint was in respect of Vojo Kupresanin calling the Captain First Class Radan?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Captain First Class Bulajic from Mrkonjic Grad was in my ammunition depot in Mrkonjic Grad, and there were allegedly some problems, that he was carrying flags and that he was forming some kind of an organisation or organising in some way within the unit, and this is what was discussed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And was the --

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the details.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But can you remember this: Was the reference to Vojo Kupresanin that it was Vojo Kupresanin who was inciting this captain to do these activities?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't think there is anything in here that says anything about anybody inciting anybody. I think that's Ms. Korner's spin on it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I agree, Your Honour, but what I'm trying to understand is what it is that Vojo Kupresanin was alleged to have done.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And he's now told her twice that he doesn't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, he hasn't, Your Honour, with respect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Put the question again. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What was your understanding of what Vojo Kupresanin's calling this captain had to do with what the man you were interviewing was complaining about?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I took it as a criticism of why a politician of the rank of Vojo Kupresanin should call a captain in the ammunition depot in Mrkonjic Grad, because they have nothing official to discuss, and he took that as a problem. And it was a problem. There is a regular line of communication, which was not respected.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If Vojo Kupresanin wanted to contact someone in the army hierarchy, who should he have been dealing with?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: He should have contacted first, if he was an officer from my unit, he should have contacted me first, and explained the reasons why it was necessary to communicate, and then this would be resolved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, it's still a little bit unclear in my mind, because although according to the record here, it's Vojo Kupresanin who was calling Captain Radan, it's the interview was conducted by an army officer by Captain First Class Bulajic. So perhaps the witness could enlighten us on who would have given the authority to Captain Bulajic to interview Captain Radan. And in addition, if this Captain Radan was not interviewed by Vojo Kupresanin but by Captain Bulajic, would he stand by what he said, that they had nothing to discuss? Because it doesn't seem to me that a discussion did take place between Captain Radan and Vojo Kupresanin but between Captain Radan and Captain Bulajic and in the form of an interview.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think we better go through this entry completely.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Captain Selak, who did Vojo Kupresanin call?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: From what is written down in the diary it seems as if Kupresanin called Captain Radan who was in Mrkonjic Grad at the depot. I added -- I put a question mark here next to that conversation, and added, "Conversation by Captain First Class Bulajic." The -- talks of this kind are not permitted. They are not in accordance with the regulations. And Captain Trako noticed this and that is why he informed me about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So your record says, "Conversation," does it,"conducted by Captain First Class Bulajic"?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Who did Captain First Class Bulajic have a conversation with?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Judging by what is written, it seems as if he talked with Radan. But it is not clear to me, so I didn't really insist, because I discussed other matters with Captain Trako, so I didn't really go into any detail about this.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think, Your Honour, that's as far as we can take this.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Just finally this, though. From your knowledge of Captain First Class Radan, what were his views in respect of nationalism?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Captain Radan had a problem. He placed the SDS flag on a hill above the depot. I found the flag before that at the barracks in Mrkonjic and demanded that party flags not be hoisted in the barracks, that they had to be on buildings where this was permitted, but not in military buildings or facilities. Radan took the flag down and took it up to the hill and hoisted it up there.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. I think that is the answer. Could you tell us what the next entry refers to? "It should be made clear whether there is a place -- there is place in the Krajina which has Colonel Subotic as its Defence Minister or not."

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The captain knew that Colonel Subotic trained paramilitary formations at Manjaca, and this Subotic became the Minister of Defence of the Army of Republika Srpska. That is how I understood it from this information here. And we didn't discuss anything further about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Over the page, which is for us, the next thing he complained about was that he still believed that Biljana Plavsic had kissed Arkan?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Was that in reference to the famous incident where she was alleged to have kissed Arkan?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That refers to the incident near Brcko, because this was on television, this event.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And could you just read what the next words you put down in your notebook are after the word "Arkan"?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: "And that Izetbegovic was making deals with terrorists."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Singular or plural?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: With saboteurs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Singular or plural? Because here it's in the singular and the interpreter is saying it is in the plural, terrorists.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Or saboteurs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Or saboteurs, yeah.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wrote down a saboteur, singular.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So he was complaining to you as well about what he believed to be the activities of Mr. Izetbegovic?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And then he talked about someone calling his wife at Donji Vakuf to tell her that Muslims have been on the prowl slaughtering people, and during the same night, Serbs leave Donji Vakuf. What ethnicity was this captain's wife?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Captain Trako's wife was a Serb, from Daruvar, from Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Was he saying that somebody called Kondic was effectively telling his wife that it was Muslims going around slaughtering people?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Kondic was a NCO. He handled ammunition in Donji Vakuf.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But then he said he found it hard to see people coming to the office wearing non-JNA insignia. Was that something you yourself had noticed?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What sort of insignia are we talking about?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Insignia meaning affiliation to certain armed formations. There were party insignia, just like we, the other officers, noticed. And he said here that he found that to be very difficult for him, that people entered his office with insignia that did not belong to the Yugoslav army.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And finally, he said, "The Muslim people are certainly for Yugoslavia." You told us that you were also for a Yugoslavia. Did he share your views?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: His wife was a Serb, so he had a Yugoslav orientation, that's the way he felt. I was also in favour of Yugoslavia. He was sincere over here and that is why he stated his views clearly.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And then he -- he -- was this a fellow officer who was with you, a Mr. Stamenkovic?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Lieutenant Colonel Stamenkovic was Captain Trako's superior officer and Lieutenant Colonel Stamenkovic asked for this conversation to take place, because Trako's views differed from the official policy that was then pursued within the army.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'll come back to that in a moment, but he ended, Trako, I see, by saying that he had to pass through Donji Vakuf and some people couldn't. And then "Serbs, Croats and Muslims can and must live together in BH". Now, you say his view --

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: -- differed from the official policy that was then pursued within the army. What was the difference between his views and the official policy?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Lieutenant Colonel Stamenkovic on a few occasions informed me that he had problems with Captain Trako with regard to some matters. Trako was a specialist, an engineer for ammunition and for grenades and explosives. As an expert, he toured all the depots and warehouses and was responsible for ammunition. He saw many things that the army did, in terms of arms and ammunition issuance, and he reacted openly when he met up with officers at the command. This deviated from the official stand of the army at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Which was what?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The stand taken by the army was in favour of Yugoslavia. However, behaviour within the army at that time, in the Banja Luka Corps, in the field, in Krajina, gatherings of the members of one ethnic group only really bothered everyone who was truly in favour of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: By April of 1992, is what you're saying that, although the official policy was to stay in an ethnically-mixed Yugoslavia, the reality was that one ethnic group was being favoured by the army?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because its ethnic composition was such. 90.5 per cent of the officers were Serbs and Montenegrins, so the army stood by the people, the ethnicity that the majority of its personnel belonged to.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Now, on our same page, do you -- but also in your diary, do you -- I'm sorry, notebook -- do you record a meeting that you had arranged at the Donji Vakuf Municipal Assembly which was attended -- and also the Bugojno Municipal Assembly attended by the 30th division, commander Colonel Galic?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And I don't think I need go through it. I think you recorded that all the matters that the President raised and Galic's response to it?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And you recorded at the end of your entry your conclusions.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, I'd like you now to please have a look at a document that's dated the following day, the 14th of April. It's attachment 4 to the statement of the 13th of July, 2000.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Item 4, you mean?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, not your official book. This is a different document, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Colonel Selak. You're going to be given it.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I beg your pardon.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's dated the 14th of April. Now, this is a document I think signed on behalf of General Talic?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And it's addressed to the command of a number of different units under his command, and does it include your command at the end, logistics base?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. 993rd logistics base in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you see this document, then, at the time it was sent?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember this document, although all official correspondence was supposed to come to my desk. However, I cannot remember this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, let's have a look at the contents. It's a report on the developments of the 2nd Military District, and it states that "Anti-army propaganda has reached unprecedented dimensions. This propaganda is led by the SDA and Alija Izetbegovic personally. Since the start of April, 1992, military facilities, army flats, and army members have been targeted by paramilitary formations." Now, was that correct?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This is not true.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Then it talks about the Bosnia-Herzegovina republican Territorial Defence staff being formed by officers who betrayed the JNA. "This action was unconstitutional and illegal. Some of these subordinate staffs sided with the BH traitors. Some still have not declared which side they are on, and some have sided with the JNA." What was that a reference to?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was a reference to the following: That the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina in Sarajevo declared mobilisation of the Territorial Defence units and it had the right to do so, according to the constitution. However, the assembly of the SFRY in 1990 passed a decision that the weapons of the Territorial Defence be withdrawn into army weapons depots, which was against the constitution because Territorial Defence units were organised at the level of the republics, not at federal level.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. So is the complaint here or what's being alleged here is that the declaration by the Bosnia-Herzegovina republic was illegal and that any JNA officer who responded was behaving illegally?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Then if we look, please, at the next, the media, "Sarajevo TV in particular are run and their editorial policy is determined by our adversaries. They refuse to accept many truths and are appearances, since that would reveal their bestiality to the public." Who was Major General Talic describing as an adversary?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: He wrote the government of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and its institutions in Sarajevo. However, may I say that in this information, he is talking about what happened in the Serb Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina in the 2nd Military District and the 5th Corps. He does not talk about Bosnia-Herzegovina. He talks about the Serb Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: He uses the expression "bestiality," and I think again when describing a Colonel Karic. Was that language that you had seen before in a -- being used in an official document?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What -- since when had those sort of expressions been used?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: On Radio Banja Luka and Banja Luka Television, I heard and saw that Colonel Karic, was seriously criticised for having placed himself on the side of the Territorial Defence of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and he was always referred to as a traitor.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But the expression -- the use of the language or the use of the word "bestiality" was that the sort of word that you would expect the commander of the 5th Corps to use in an official document?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This expression is indeed most uncouth. I don't remember ever having used it in my own speech. It is most uncouth.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And finally, please, on this document, could you turn to paragraph 8?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: "Colonel Petar Spasojevic will talk to the commanders and commands of subordinated municipal Territorial Defence staffs to determine whose side they are on. Staffs that refuse to carry out orders shall be disbanded and new staffs shall be formed in their place. Written reports describing the situation in the municipal staffs shall be submitted by the 16th of April, 1992." First, under whose authority did the municipal Territorial Defence staff act?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Colonel Spasojevic was commander of the Territorial Defence staff, the joint Territorial Defence staff, and he was in charge of commanding these staffs. It is shown quite clearly here that the corps commander had the power of issuing orders, namely to command TO staffs as well, because he is giving orders to Colonel Spasojevic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Was Colonel Spasojevic a regular JNA officer?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: An active-duty officer. For a while, he was commander of the armoured brigade in Banja Luka. He's a Serb.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And in asking whose side they are on, what did you understand that to mean?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That they should be ethnically established, that they should be Serb staffs without Muslims and Croats.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And then finally, on the last page, is there a distribution list?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Handwritten?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Somebody wrote on the last page who copies were sent to.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay. Does that include what is described as the Volunteer Battalion?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Do you know what that Volunteer Battalion was?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I mean, I knew that it existed but where it was located is something that I never found out.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. That's all we need with that document.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That's P1578, please. I would now like to go back, please, to your notebook, work record, whatever one is calling it. Could we go, please, to the 28th of April, please?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And you had a meeting, did you there, with the assistant commander?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Was that Colonel Bosko Kelecevic?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And there is a discussion there about a replacement of a Lieutenant Colonel Mujagic, whose life had been threatened. Further down, the request apparently came from the depot soldiers. What nationality was Lieutenant Colonel Mujagic?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Lieutenant Colonel Mujagic was a Muslim, a Bosniak. He had a master of sciences degree in the technical sciences.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And his life had apparently been threatened. By whom had his life been threatened?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: His soldiers at the Krcmarica arms depot near Banja Luka, whose commander he was, made these threats.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, I want now to deal with the topic of the dismissals from the army and the, as it were, exodus of non-Serbs from the army. This is dated the 28th of April. Before that, had there been threats made to officers of non-Serb ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were quite a few threats. People felt unsafe. Information was received that officers who were Croats and Bosniaks would have to leave the army in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and that they were going to Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And what were they going to Belgrade for?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: To get new assignments, at the headquarters of the army of Yugoslavia. They were deployed to menial jobs.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, I want to start with a letter that you yourself wrote to the 2nd Military District commander.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could he be handed that -- I don't know. It went with a collection of newspaper articles, I think, but it's got a number in the translation, of 00349310. Your Honour, we've got a spare copy here but I think the Registrar is having difficulty. Usher, if you take that place it on the ELMO because Mr. Ackerman doesn't have it.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the Presiding Judge, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you have it, Mr. Ackerman? Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We've given our copy to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's not got a date on it, Colonel Selak, although we can see it must have been sometime in May because it refers to articles. Can you remember roughly when you wrote it?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was the beginning of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think there is definitely a mistake. I've noticed that one in the translation, that even I understand B/C/S, to be the 26th of March, March, not May, I think. But anyhow, we'll read through it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What you wrote, Colonel Selak, was this: "To the 2nd Military District commander." Was that still General Kukanjac?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: "I am applying to you as my commander not to protect my life and the lives of my family because you cannot help me in that but to plead for the protection of your officers' dignity, to demand that the JNA protect its members from certain political parties which have the audacity to openly threaten and order the members of other ethnic groups to leave the army." I'm going to pause there because we'll see what you were talking about in a moment. "I have been subjected to similar threats before, but by the end of last March, the threats to my person from the Banja Luka SDS leaders became blatantly public. For instance, in the Banja Luka Glas daily of 26th of March, and 6th April, and the Banja Luka Radio on the 5th of April, 1992. I have enclosed a copy of the article." What's the date there, 26th of what?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 26th of April, no, no, no. The 5th. March, March, yes, March. It was a slip.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's been wrongly translated in the -- in the 26th of March edition, the same publication called all the JNA general staff traitors, and in particular, "General Adzic, acting federal secretary for national defence. Identical threats have been addressed to several Croat, Slovene and Muslim officers. Is it possible that we are being called traitors, are being denounced for not being loyal officers, whereas we could become the nucleus for and an encouragement to other members of our ethnic groups who must be recruited if we wish the army to remain a Yugoslav army and become a nucleus around which a new union of Yugoslav peoples could be created? If my organisation should fail to defend me, I am afraid that my friends, people who know me, or even my colleagues from the JNA will conclude that I must be a traitor to this army after all. I have known and respected -- I have known you and respected you for a long time. That is why I am writing to you, even though I know that you must have more important concerns on your mind. Still, I ask that you believe me when I say that this is not a small matter either. Please accept the assurance of my respect." Did you ever receive a response to your letter from the general?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, may that then be made, please, Exhibit P1579? And can we now look at the articles? Your Honour, the first is headed, "The treachery of the general staff." It doesn't have a date in the top, but it's Banja Luka 17th of March. And the subject is, "BH, SDS officials call for removal of some army officers."

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can you, Colonel Selak, please find the part of -- this is -- I'm not sure we know what the publication is, but I think it's Glas because I think we will see this gentleman writes for Glas?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What's the date, Banja Luka what, is it the 27th of March?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Banja Luka, the 27th of March, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, this is describing a news conference held today by, that day, by Dr. Vukic, who was president of the regional board of the SDS. Did you know Dr. Vukic? Had you met Dr. Vukic?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I knew him personally.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: He said that, "After Mesic" - is that Stipe Mesic - "Izetbegovic was the second author, scenarist and director of Serbian death." To continue, "The Yugoslav army, an internal aggressor is no different to the base behaviour."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] English, English. I don't have a translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is it okay now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's okay now. It's okay now.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think we will leave that part. "Vukic said stressing that the Serbian people of Bosanska Krajina and Bosnia-Herzegovina have been sacrificed according to the same principle as the Serbian people in the Serbian autonomous district of Krajina. The greatest treachery has come from the general staff of the Yugoslav People's Army," Vukic claimed. In his opinion, this is because "those who started the war and forced Serbian children into the whirl wind of war are now peacemakers," et cetera. "The fact is the JNA no longer exists and it is also a fact that Serbian children make up 90 per cent of the active combat forces of the army which remains," and so on. "Only the Banja Luka Corps remains - Dr. Vukic said - and many people, including General Vasilavic, consider it to be the core of the SDS. It is actually a SDS corps because it is made up of Serbs and will be even more so when some officers are removed from the military command, the Banja Luka Corps, and are sent home." Pausing there, Colonel Selak, by March the 27th, was that in your view an accurate statement, that the Banja Luka Corps had become effectively an SDS corps?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: "Colonel" I continue reading, "And little colonels from the unsuccessful battlefields cannot be brought here because various Hasotics, Selaks, and Ludinacs have been brought in to destroy the Banja Luka Corps and impose themselves before Major General Momir Talic, who is the only bright part of the Banja Luka Corps, Dr. Vukic said." And I think we can leave out the next sentence. "According to the President of the SDS regional board, the SDS, the Banja Luka Corps, and the Serbian people of the Bosanska Krajina must help Major General Talic survive the deceits in his command from the failed generals in the general staff who have the assignment of destroying the fabric of the Banja Luka Corps." And I don't think that we need trouble with the end. Now, the -- you and Colonel Hasotic who I think -- perhaps you better tell us what his position was because I'm not sure I've asked you about him before. What was his position in the Banja Luka Corps?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Colonel Hasotic, before this, was General Mladic's deputy for morale in Knin, and he was performing the same duty in the Banja Luka Corps until early August, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And who was Ludinac?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ludvik, he was Colonel Ludvik Kranjc. He was the chief of the military academy in Banja Luka. And at this time, when this was written, he was in the Banja Luka Corps, in the corps command, and he was part of Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. the operative and training department, he was from Slovenia.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So he was a Slovenian. And what was Colonel Hasotic?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was born in Sandzak, in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And by ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: A Bosniak.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Was this the first time that you and these other gentlemen had been the -- or the demand effectively -- no, I'm sorry, can I rephrase that question completely? Was this the first time you had been publicly named by the SDS as potential destroyers of the Banja Luka Corps?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This is not the first time the media, especially the Banja Luka Glas, on several occasions wrote in a very nasty way about me.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So before the 27th of March?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were also threats made over the telephone.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The fact that the leader of the SDS in Banja Luka, Dr. Vukic, or the President of the regional board of the SDS, was calling you destroyers publicly, in fact at a meeting, was that something that was going to be -- have an effect?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It could have had a very negative affect on all of us who are mentioned here because the citizens of Banja Luka could have carried out an assassination or other threats. There could have been other negative repercussions for us and for our families, and that was a sign for other officers as well, Croats, Bosniaks and Slovenians to leave the army, which is what happened later.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour could that be made Exhibit P15890 -- 1580? And that is I think it for today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Colonel, that is not it for you. We will continue tomorrow. As you have been informed, we will also continue on Monday. So we will reconvene tomorrow morning at 9.00, all right? Tomorrow morning at 9.00. Thank you.
